questions.q: One mole of any substance contains
questions.explanation: A mole contains Avogadro's number, 6.022 × 10^23, of atoms, molecules or ions.

questions.q: 10 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 90 g of water. What is the mass percent of sodium chloride in the solution?
What is the mass of 3.011 × 10^23 molecules of water? (H2O = 18 g/mol; NA = 6.022 × 10^23 per mol)
questions.explanation: 3.011 × 10^23 molecules is 0.5 mol, so mass = 0.5 × 18 = 9 g.

questions.q: What volume of 0.2 M NaOH solution is needed to neutralise 20 mL of 0.1 M HCl?
questions.explanation: Moles of HCl = 0.020 × 0.1 = 0.002 mol, and the volume of 0.2 M NaOH = 0.002/0.2 = 0.01 L = 10 mL.

questions.q: 10 g of calcium carbonate is heated and gives 5.6 g of calcium oxide. By the law of conservation of mass, what mass of carbon dioxide is released?
questions.explanation: Mass of reactant equals mass of products, so CO2 = 10 - 5.6 = 4.4 g.

questions.q: A 1.22 g sample of hydrated barium chloride, BaCl2·xH2O, loses 0.18 g of water on heating. What is x? (Ba = 137, Cl = 35.5, H2O = 18)
Distinguish between molarity and molality, and state which one changes with temperature.
questions.answer: Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution; molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Molarity changes with temperature because the volume changes, whereas molality does not because mass is independent of temperature.
keyPoints: Molarity = mol per litre of solution
Molality = mol per kg of solvent
Only molarity depends on temperature
questions.explanation: Volumes expand on heating but masses stay the same, so molality is preferred where temperature varies.

questions.q: What volume of carbon dioxide at 273 K and 1 atm is produced by the complete combustion of 6 g of carbon? (C = 12; molar volume 22.4 L/mol)
keyPoints: C + O2 → CO2, 1 mol C gives 1 mol CO2
6 g C = 0.5 mol
questions.explanation: The mole ratio of C to CO2 is 1 : 1, so 0.5 mol of CO2 is formed.

questions.q: The nucleus of an atom contains
questions.explanation: The nucleus holds protons and neutrons (nucleons), while electrons move outside it.

questions.q: The spectral series of hydrogen that lies in the visible region is the
questions.explanation: The Balmer series, which ends at n = 2, has lines in the visible region.

questions.q: The Lyman series of the hydrogen spectrum lies in which region?
questions.explanation: Lyman lines arise from transitions to n = 1 and involve the largest energy gaps, which gives ultraviolet radiation.

questions.q: How many radial nodes does a 2s orbital have?
questions.explanation: Radial nodes = n - l - 1 = 2 - 0 - 1 = 1.

questions.q: What is the shape of a p orbital?
questions.explanation: A p orbital has two lobes on opposite sides of the nucleus, which gives a dumb-bell shape.

questions.q: Which of the following electron configurations is impossible?
questions.explanation: The 2p subshell has 3 orbitals, so by the Pauli exclusion principle it can hold at most 6 electrons, not 7.

questions.q: Give two reasons why Bohr's model is inadequate for atoms other than hydrogen.
questions.answer: It cannot explain the spectra of multi-electron atoms and cannot explain the splitting of lines in electric and magnetic fields; it also ignores the wave nature of electrons and violates the uncertainty principle.
keyPoints: Fails for multi-electron atoms
Cannot explain fine structure or Zeeman and Stark effects
Ignores dual nature of matter and the uncertainty principle
questions.explanation: The quantum mechanical model replaced it.

questions.q: How many photons of wavelength 500 nm are emitted per second by a 1 W source of such light? (h = 6.626 × 10^-34 J s, c = 3 × 10^8 m/s)
keyPoints: Energy of one photon = hc/λ = 3.98 × 10^-19 J
Power 1 W = 1 J per second
questions.explanation: Photons per second equal total energy per second divided by the energy of one photon.

questions.q: Which of the following is a metalloid?
questions.explanation: Silicon has properties between those of metals and non-metals, so it is a metalloid.

questions.q: The elements of group 17 are called
questions.explanation: Group 17 (F, Cl, Br, I, At) elements are the halogens.

questions.q: Which of the elements Be, Mg, Ca and Ba has the highest metallic character?
questions.explanation: Metallic character increases down a group, so barium is the most metallic.

questions.q: Which of the following elements of the third period has the largest atomic radius?
questions.explanation: Atomic radius decreases across a period, so sodium at the left end is the largest.

questions.q: Beryllium resembles aluminium (a diagonal relationship). Which property do both elements share?
options: Both form amphoteric oxides and hydroxides
Both have the same atomic radius
questions.explanation: BeO and Al2O3 are amphoteric, and both metals form covalent chlorides and are rendered passive by concentrated nitric acid.

questions.q: Which of the elements Mg, Al, Na and Si has the highest second ionisation enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Removing the second electron from Na+ breaks the stable noble gas core 2s2 2p6, which needs far more energy than removing the second electron from the others.

questions.q: Define first ionisation enthalpy and name two factors that affect it.
questions.answer: It is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from an isolated gaseous atom in its ground state. It depends on atomic size, nuclear charge, shielding by inner electrons, and the stability of the electron configuration.
keyPoints: Energy to remove one electron from a gaseous atom
Depends on atomic radius and nuclear charge
Also on shielding and filled or half-filled stability
questions.explanation: A small atom with high effective nuclear charge has a high ionisation enthalpy.

questions.q: Account for the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium.
questions.answer: Li+ and Mg2+ have similar charge-to-radius ratios (polarising power), because moving down a group increases size while moving right increases charge; hence both form covalent compounds and nitrides and have similar solubilities.
keyPoints: Similar ionic potential (charge/size)
Both form nitrides with nitrogen
Similar solubility and covalent character of compounds
questions.explanation: Size increases down a group and charge increases across a period, so the effects nearly cancel diagonally.

questions.q: Which carbon-carbon bond has the highest bond enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Bond enthalpy increases with bond order, and the triple bond is strongest.

questions.q: The bond between hydrogen and chlorine in HCl is
questions.explanation: The electrons are shared unequally because chlorine is more electronegative than hydrogen.

questions.q: What is the H-C-H bond angle in methane?
questions.explanation: The four sp3 bonds point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron, at 109.5 degrees.

questions.q: In which of the following molecules does the central atom have an incomplete octet?
questions.explanation: Boron in BF3 has only six electrons around it, while the central atoms in the others have eight.

questions.q: What is the total number of valence electrons in one molecule of ammonia, NH3?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen contributes 5 and three hydrogens contribute 1 each, giving 8.

questions.q: Which of the following molecules is non-polar although it contains polar bonds?
questions.explanation: CCl4 is tetrahedral and symmetrical, so its four C-Cl bond dipoles cancel.

questions.q: What is resonance? Illustrate with ozone.
questions.answer: Resonance is the representation of a molecule by two or more Lewis structures that differ only in electron arrangement; the real molecule is a hybrid. In ozone the two O-O bonds are identical, with each lying between a single and a double bond.
keyPoints: Several contributing structures differ in electron positions
Actual structure is a resonance hybrid
Ozone: two equal O-O bonds
questions.explanation: The hybrid is more stable than any single contributing structure.

questions.q: CO2 and SO2 both have the formula AX2 but CO2 is linear and SO2 is bent. Explain.
questions.answer: The central carbon in CO2 has two bond pairs and no lone pair, so the molecule is linear. Sulphur in SO2 has two bond pairs and one lone pair, so lone pair repulsion makes the molecule bent.
keyPoints: CO2: no lone pair on carbon, linear
SO2: one lone pair on sulphur
Lone pair repulsion bends the molecule
questions.explanation: Shape depends on both bond pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.

questions.q: Which instrument is used to measure atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

questions.q: What is the value of 1 atm in pascal?
questions.explanation: 1 atm = 101 325 Pa, or about 1.013 × 10^5 Pa.

questions.q: Water rises in a narrow glass capillary tube because of
options: surface tension and the adhesion of water to the glass
questions.explanation: Adhesion between water and glass is stronger than cohesion in water, and surface tension pulls the liquid up the tube.

questions.q: Evaporation of a liquid causes cooling because
options: heat is added to the surroundings
the most energetic molecules escape, lowering the average kinetic energy of the rest
questions.explanation: Only the fastest molecules can leave the surface, so the average kinetic energy, and hence temperature, of the liquid drops.

questions.q: What is 25 °C expressed on the kelvin scale?
At the same temperature and pressure, what is the ratio of the density of oxygen gas to that of hydrogen gas?
questions.explanation: At the same T and P, density is proportional to molar mass, so 32/2 = 16.

questions.q: What volume is occupied by 0.5 mol of an ideal gas at 2 atm and 300 K? (R = 0.0821 L atm K^-1 mol^-1)
State Boyle's law and write its mathematical form.
questions.answer: At constant temperature, the pressure of a fixed mass of gas is inversely proportional to its volume: P ∝ 1/V, or P1V1 = P2V2.
keyPoints: Constant temperature and fixed mass
Pressure inversely proportional to volume
P1V1 = P2V2
questions.explanation: The product PV stays constant for an ideal gas at fixed T.

questions.q: Why do real gases deviate more from ideal behaviour at low temperatures?
questions.answer: At low temperature the molecules move slowly, so the attractive forces between them can no longer be ignored; the gas then occupies a smaller volume than predicted and the ideal gas law fails.
keyPoints: Lower kinetic energy of molecules
Intermolecular attractions become significant
Gas liquefies near its boiling point
questions.explanation: The ideal gas model assumes the molecules do not attract each other.

questions.q: What is the unit of molar entropy?
questions.explanation: Entropy has units of energy per kelvin, so molar entropy is J K^-1 mol^-1.

questions.q: A calorimeter is used to measure
options: heat changes in chemical or physical processes
questions.explanation: A calorimeter measures the heat absorbed or released in a reaction, from the temperature change of a known mass of water.

questions.q: The enthalpy of combustion of a substance is always
options: dependent on the sign of ΔS
questions.explanation: Combustion releases heat, so the enthalpy change is negative.

questions.q: What standard pressure is used for thermodynamic data under the current IUPAC recommendation?
questions.explanation: The standard state pressure is 1 bar (10^5 Pa).

questions.q: Which of the following has the highest molar entropy?
questions.explanation: Gases are the most disordered state, so steam has the highest entropy.

questions.q: The enthalpy of atomisation of methane, CH4(g) → C(g) + 4H(g), is 1660 kJ/mol. What is the average C-H bond enthalpy?
questions.explanation: Four C-H bonds are broken, so the average bond enthalpy = 1660/4 = 415 kJ/mol.

questions.q: For the reaction C(s) + O2(g) → CO2(g), the difference ΔH - ΔU is
questions.explanation: Δng = 1 - 1 = 0, so ΔH = ΔU + ΔngRT = ΔU.

questions.q: Define internal energy. Is it a state function?
questions.answer: Internal energy is the total of all kinetic and potential energies of the particles of a system. It is a state function, because its change depends only on the initial and final states and not on the path.
keyPoints: Sum of all energies of the molecules
State function
Change depends only on initial and final states
questions.explanation: Heat and work separately are path functions, but q + w = ΔU is not.

questions.q: Show that the heat absorbed at constant pressure equals the change in enthalpy.
questions.answer: From ΔU = q + w with w = -PΔV at constant pressure, q = ΔU + PΔV. Since H = U + PV, ΔH = ΔU + PΔV at constant pressure, so qp = ΔH.
keyPoints: ΔU = q + w, w = -PΔV
q = ΔU + PΔV
ΔH = ΔU + PΔV, so qp = ΔH
questions.explanation: Enthalpy was defined so that heat at constant pressure is a state function.

questions.q: According to the Brønsted-Lowry theory, an acid is
questions.explanation: A Brønsted-Lowry acid donates a proton (H+) to another species.

questions.q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 °C?
questions.explanation: In pure water [H+] = 10^-7 M, so pH = 7.

questions.q: A solution of pH 3 has how many times the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution of pH 5?
questions.explanation: pH differs by 2 units, so the [H+] differs by 10^2 = 100 times.

questions.q: A very large value of Kc for a reaction means that at equilibrium
options: reactants and products are present in equal amounts
questions.explanation: Kc is the ratio of product to reactant concentrations, so a large Kc means the reaction goes nearly to completion.

questions.q: Which of the following mixtures acts as an alkaline buffer?
questions.explanation: A weak base with its salt with a strong acid resists changes in pH on the alkaline side.

questions.q: For N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g), the relation between Kp and Kc is
questions.explanation: Kp = Kc (RT)^Δng and Δng = 2 - 4 = -2.

questions.q: The Ksp of AgCl is 1.8 × 10^-10. What is its solubility in 0.1 M NaCl solution (ignoring the Cl- from AgCl)?
questions.explanation: [Ag+] = Ksp/[Cl-] = 1.8 × 10^-10 / 0.1 = 1.8 × 10^-9 M, far lower than in pure water.

questions.q: Define a Lewis acid and a Lewis base with one example of each.
questions.answer: A Lewis acid is an electron pair acceptor (for example BF3), and a Lewis base is an electron pair donor (for example NH3).
keyPoints: Acid accepts an electron pair
Base donates an electron pair
Examples: BF3 acid, NH3 base
questions.explanation: The Lewis definition covers reactions without protons, such as BF3 + NH3 → F3B-NH3.

questions.q: The synthesis of ammonia, N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, is exothermic (ΔH = -92 kJ/mol). Why is a moderate temperature of about 700 K used in industry rather than a very low one?
questions.answer: A low temperature favours a higher yield of ammonia, but the rate becomes too slow; a moderate temperature (with a catalyst and high pressure) is a compromise between rate and yield.
keyPoints: Exothermic reaction: low temperature favours yield
Low temperature makes the rate too slow
Compromise temperature with catalyst gives acceptable rate and yield
questions.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle gives the direction of shift, while kinetics decides how fast equilibrium is reached.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of sodium in NaCl?
questions.explanation: Alkali metals always have an oxidation number of +1 in their compounds.

questions.q: An oxidising agent
questions.explanation: An oxidising agent takes electrons from another species and is itself reduced.

questions.q: What is the oxidation number of chlorine in sodium hypochlorite, NaClO?
What is the oxidation number of nitrogen in nitric acid, HNO3?
Which of the following reactions will take place?
questions.explanation: Iron is above copper in the activity series, so it displaces copper; the other reactions would need a less reactive metal to displace a more reactive one.

questions.q: In which of the following compounds does nitrogen have the oxidation number +4?
questions.explanation: The oxidation numbers of nitrogen are +4 in NO2, +1 in N2O, +2 in NO and +5 in N2O5.

questions.q: In acidic solution, how many moles of KMnO4 are needed to oxidise 5 mol of Fe2+ to Fe3+?
questions.explanation: Each MnO4- accepts 5 electrons (Mn +7 to +2), and each Fe2+ gives 1 electron, so 5 mol Fe2+ needs 1 mol MnO4-.

questions.q: What is a displacement reaction? Give an example involving a metal.
questions.answer: A displacement reaction is one in which a more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound; for example Zn + CuSO4 → ZnSO4 + Cu.
keyPoints: More reactive element displaces a less reactive one
Is a redox reaction
Example: zinc and copper sulphate
questions.explanation: Zinc is oxidised (0 to +2) and copper ions are reduced (+2 to 0).

questions.q: Nitrous acid, HNO2, can act as both an oxidising and a reducing agent. Explain.
questions.answer: Nitrogen in HNO2 has oxidation number +3, which is intermediate between its possible range (-3 to +5), so it can be reduced (for example to NO) or oxidised (for example to HNO3).
keyPoints: Oxidation number of N is +3
Intermediate oxidation state
Can be oxidised to +5 or reduced to lower values
questions.explanation: A species with an intermediate oxidation state can either gain or lose electrons.

questions.q: Which is the most abundant isotope of hydrogen?
questions.explanation: Protium (1H) makes up over 99.98% of natural hydrogen.

questions.q: Which alkali metal has a melting point close to room temperature (about 28.5 °C)?
questions.explanation: Caesium has the lowest melting point among the alkali metals and melts just above room temperature.

questions.q: What is the formula of caustic soda?
questions.explanation: Caustic soda is sodium hydroxide, NaOH.

questions.q: Bleaching powder is prepared by passing chlorine gas over
questions.explanation: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 → Ca(OCl)Cl + H2O, giving bleaching powder (CaOCl2).

questions.q: Which s-block element is present in chlorophyll?
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll has a magnesium ion at the centre of its porphyrin ring.

questions.q: In Clark's method, temporary hardness of water is removed by adding
options: a calculated amount of slaked lime
questions.explanation: Ca(OH)2 reacts with Ca(HCO3)2 to give insoluble CaCO3, which is filtered off.

questions.q: What volume of hydrogen gas at 273 K and 1 atm is produced when 2.3 g of sodium reacts with excess water? (Na = 23; molar volume 22.4 L/mol)
questions.explanation: 2Na + 2H2O → 2NaOH + H2, so 0.1 mol Na gives 0.05 mol H2 = 1.12 L.

questions.q: State two ways in which lithium differs from the other alkali metals.
questions.answer: Lithium is harder and has a higher melting point; it forms a nitride with nitrogen and its carbonate, hydroxide and nitrate decompose on heating more easily, and LiCl is deliquescent and soluble in organic solvents.
keyPoints: Forms Li3N with nitrogen
Compounds are more covalent and less thermally stable
Harder and higher melting point
questions.explanation: The differences are due to the very small size and high polarising power of Li+.

questions.q: How does the electrolysis of molten sodium hydride show that it contains the hydride ion, H-?
questions.answer: Hydrogen gas is liberated at the anode, which shows that hydrogen is present as the negative ion H-, which is oxidised at the positive electrode.
keyPoints: Molten NaH conducts electricity
Hydrogen is released at the anode
Anions migrate to the anode, so H- is the anion
questions.explanation: At the anode 2H- → H2 + 2e-.

questions.q: Which gas is commonly used in fire extinguishers?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is non-combustible and heavier than air, so it smothers fires.

questions.q: Carborundum is the common name of
questions.explanation: Carborundum is silicon carbide, SiC, an extremely hard abrasive.

questions.q: Among the boron trihalides, which is the strongest Lewis acid?
questions.explanation: Back bonding is strongest in BF3 (similar-sized 2p orbitals) and weakest in BBr3, so BBr3 is the most electron-deficient and the strongest acid.

questions.q: Graphite is used for electrodes because it
questions.explanation: Delocalised electrons between its layers make graphite a good conductor, and it is also chemically inert.

questions.q: In the thermite reaction, aluminium acts as
questions.explanation: In 2Al + Fe2O3 → Al2O3 + 2Fe, aluminium is oxidised and reduces the iron(III) oxide.

questions.q: The B-F bond length in BF3 is shorter than expected for a single bond because of
options: pπ-pπ back bonding from fluorine to boron
questions.explanation: Fluorine donates a lone pair into boron's empty 2p orbital, giving partial double-bond character.

questions.q: SiCl4 fumes in moist air because
options: it is hydrolysed to give HCl and silicic acid
questions.explanation: SiCl4 + 4H2O → Si(OH)4 + 4HCl, and the HCl forms fumes in damp air.

questions.q: Write the equation for the laboratory preparation of diborane from boron trifluoride.
keyPoints: Boron trifluoride treated with lithium aluminium hydride
Dry ether solvent
Products include diborane, LiF and AlF3
questions.explanation: The hydride transfers H- ions to boron, forming B2H6.

questions.q: Why are lead(IV) compounds such as PbO2 strong oxidising agents?
questions.answer: Because of the inert pair effect, Pb(II) is more stable than Pb(IV), so Pb(IV) readily gains two electrons to become Pb(II) and oxidises other substances.
keyPoints: Inert pair effect
Pb(II) more stable than Pb(IV)
Pb(IV) accepts electrons to form Pb(II)
questions.explanation: PbO2 is used as the oxidising electrode in the lead storage battery.

questions.q: The unique property of carbon that allows it to form long chains by linking with itself is called
questions.explanation: Catenation is the ability of atoms of the same element to bond together to form chains and rings.

questions.q: The -COOH group is the functional group of
questions.explanation: -COOH is the carboxyl group present in carboxylic acids.

questions.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-CH=CH2?
questions.explanation: A three-carbon chain with one double bond is propene.

questions.q: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
questions.explanation: In propan-2-ol the carbon bearing -OH is attached to two other carbon atoms.

questions.q: How many alpha (adjacent C-H) hydrogens can take part in hyperconjugation in the tert-butyl carbocation, (CH3)3C+?
questions.explanation: The positive carbon is attached to three methyl groups, each with 3 hydrogens, giving 9.

questions.q: A carbocation is
questions.explanation: The positively charged carbon has three sigma bonds and an empty p orbital, so it is trigonal planar and sp2.

questions.q: How many structural isomers that are alcohols have the molecular formula C4H10O?
questions.explanation: They are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

questions.q: Distinguish between an electrophile and a nucleophile with one example each.
questions.answer: An electrophile is an electron-deficient species that accepts an electron pair (for example NO2+ or H+), whereas a nucleophile is an electron-rich species that donates an electron pair (for example OH- or CN-).
keyPoints: Electrophile: electron pair acceptor, e.g. NO2+
Nucleophile: electron pair donor, e.g. OH-
They react with each other
questions.explanation: Most polar organic reactions involve a nucleophile attacking an electron-poor carbon.

questions.q: In paper chromatography a spot moves 3 cm while the solvent front moves 6 cm. Define the Rf value and calculate it.
questions.answer: Rf is the ratio of the distance moved by the compound to the distance moved by the solvent front; here Rf = 3/6 = 0.5.
keyPoints: Rf = distance moved by spot / distance moved by solvent front
3 cm / 6 cm
Rf = 0.5 (always less than 1)
questions.explanation: Rf is characteristic of a compound for a given solvent and paper, so it helps identify substances.

questions.q: Which gas is the main constituent of natural gas?
questions.explanation: Natural gas is mostly methane, usually over 80 to 90 percent.

questions.q: Which of the following is an aromatic hydrocarbon?
questions.explanation: Benzene has a planar ring with delocalised pi electrons, which makes it aromatic.

questions.q: How many pi bonds are there in a Kekulé structure of benzene?
questions.explanation: The ring has three alternating C=C double bonds, each containing one pi bond.

questions.q: Ethene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of finely divided nickel to give
questions.explanation: Catalytic hydrogenation converts the double bond to a single bond, giving ethane.

questions.q: Ethyne reacts with excess hydrogen in the presence of nickel to give
questions.explanation: Both pi bonds of the triple bond are hydrogenated, giving ethane (ethene is the intermediate).

questions.q: Addition of HCl to 2-methylpropene gives mainly
questions.explanation: By Markovnikov's rule the more stable tertiary carbocation forms, so chlorine attaches to the tertiary carbon.

questions.q: Benzene does not decolourise bromine water because
options: its delocalised pi electron system gives extra stability, so it resists addition
it is insoluble in all liquids
questions.explanation: Addition would destroy the aromatic stabilisation, so benzene reacts only by substitution under suitable catalysis.

questions.q: Write the balanced equation for the complete combustion of ethyne.
keyPoints: Products are CO2 and H2O
Balanced with 4 C, 4 H and 10 O
Burns with a sooty, luminous flame because of high carbon content
questions.explanation: Ethyne burns with a very hot flame, which is used in oxy-acetylene welding.

questions.q: How can you distinguish ethyne from ethene using a simple chemical test?
questions.answer: Ethyne, having an acidic terminal hydrogen, gives a white precipitate of silver acetylide with ammoniacal silver nitrate solution (Tollens' reagent), whereas ethene gives no precipitate.
keyPoints: Terminal alkynes have acidic hydrogen
White precipitate of silver acetylide with ammoniacal AgNO3
Ethene gives no precipitate
questions.explanation: Only terminal alkynes (R-C≡C-H) show this test.
